title: The Problem of Extreme Complexity
coreMove: Spot when a system has become too complex to trust to memory and individual command alone.
sourcePressure: The source uses the Austrian drowning rescue, the era of superspecialists, and the limits of lone mastery to diagnose why avoidable failure persists inside expert work before checklists appear as a response.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version says smart people should try harder to remember the basics. The real chapter says the structure has outgrown unaided memory.

sourceAnchors.name: Austrian drowning rescue
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar identifies the Austrian drowning rescue as the opening concrete case for a chain of precise coordinated actions under pressure.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The Austrian rescue matters because the save lives in the chain, not in one brilliant pair of hands.

sourceAnchors.name: the era of superspecialists
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar ties the chapter to modern medicine's superspecialists and the new handoff burden created by narrower expertise.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Superspecialists make medicine more powerful and more dependent on the seams between them.

hook: A busy hospital proves checklists are useful
counterintuition: The problem is not knowledge, it is execution
tryThisNow: Write down three steps you often forget
Make a quick checklist for tomorrow

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.domain: Sarah, a trauma nurse in a winter rescue handoff
exampleSpecs.audience: clinicians who assume skill covers every transition
exampleSpecs.stakes: a hypothermia patient loses time if one warm-fluid setup is assumed instead of owned
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Sarah tags each handoff on the trauma bay wall and finds the unowned warm-fluid step before the patient leaves the ambulance stretcher
exampleSpecs.firstImage: meltwater dripping from a yellow rescue blanket onto the trauma bay floor
mustAvoid: hero nurse saves the day alone

exampleSpecs.domain: Mathieu, an urban rail signal maintainer during overnight work
exampleSpecs.audience: technical teams with many expert roles in one narrow window
exampleSpecs.stakes: a morning commuter shutdown if power isolation and signal testing pass each other unseen
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Mathieu maps the work window by owner, not task type, and exposes the one test nobody has claimed
exampleSpecs.firstImage: orange work lamps reflecting on wet rails in an empty station

exampleSpecs.domain: Ingrid, a specialty pharmacy coordinator handling transplant orders
exampleSpecs.audience: health administrators who see errors as staff attentiveness problems
exampleSpecs.stakes: a transplant patient misses a narrow medication delivery window
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Ingrid rebuilds the missed order path across prescriber, insurer, courier, and cold storage instead of blaming the last person who touched the screen
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a cold-pack label curling at the edge of an empty pharmacy tote

exampleSpecs.domain: James, a youth sailing regatta safety officer
exampleSpecs.audience: volunteer leaders coordinating weather, boats, and children
exampleSpecs.stakes: a storm line arrives while adults believe another boat has counted the beginners
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: James asks which adult owns the beginner headcount and reveals that three adults each thought another clipboard held it
exampleSpecs.firstImage: gray wind flattening the flags along the dock

exampleSpecs.domain: Sofia, a museum conservation lead moving a fragile crate
exampleSpecs.audience: project leads who mistake expertise in each specialty for control of the whole move
exampleSpecs.stakes: a cracked artifact if lift timing, humidity, and loading dock access do not line up
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Sofia stops the crate move until each specialist states the one dependency they need from the next person
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Who owns the dock door?" Sofia asks while the crate straps hang loose

exampleSpecs.domain: Hadiya, a municipal snow emergency dispatcher
exampleSpecs.audience: operations managers who trust experience during peak load
exampleSpecs.stakes: ambulance access to a hill street depends on plow routing, salt supply, and police closure timing
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Hadiya circles the street where three departments overlap and names it as an omission risk before the calls arrive
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You watch blue plow dots crawl across a dispatch map while the radio queue grows

skillTargets: spot when distributed expertise needs a support
evaluate whether a proposed fix preserves judgment

tryThisNowSpec: Name one live workflow with three or more owners, then write the single step most likely to be assumed rather than owned.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
